target_customer: Smartphone shoppers, mostly women, browsing fashion inspiration and buying through an app, with retailers paying through affiliate links
problem: Shopping on phones lacked discovery and inspiration. Inporia built Kaleidoscope, an ecommerce inspiration app and widget, as the first of a planned series of ecommerce apps.
business_model: Consumer ecommerce discovery app, presumably affiliate or commission revenue (not stated in sources)
product_category: Mobile ecommerce and fashion inspiration app

founders.name: Ryan Junee
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (May 2011) calls him a serial entrepreneur, former YouTube product manager and advisor to 500 Startups and StartMate. The YC page says former Googler and Omnisio co-founder.

founders.name: Max Skibinsky
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (May 2011) calls him a gaming veteran who sold Hive7 to Playdom in 2010. The YC description names him as co-founder.

exit.reason: Cause and date not public. Dealroom lists the company as closed and CB Insights as dead. Kaleidoscope was still being covered in August 2012.

competitors.name: Decide
competitors.what: Seattle ecommerce startup that raised funding before launch, cited by TechCrunch as a comparable

competitors.name: Snapette
competitors.what: Mobile app for browsing and sharing in-store fashion finds by location, beta in August 2011

technical_complexity.rationale: Mobile apps for Android and iPhone plus a widget and some machine learning for recommendations. Standard engineering for a team with game and web veterans.

defensibility.rationale: Fashion inspiration feeds were easy to copy and Pinterest, Fancy and others were already crowded the category (Mashable, April 2012).

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Pinterest grew rapidly in 2011 to 2012 and added shopping features. No acquisition of Inporia was found.

market_need_then: Mobile commerce was growing in 2011 and investors including NEA and SV Angel funded the stealth seed. Mashable said in April 2012 the world did not need another fashion inspiration app, which shows crowding.

branding.domain_note: inporia.com did not load during research (HTTP 445).

identity.visual_style: Kaleidoscope was a curated street style look browsing app (TNW and Mashable, 2012)

branding.brand_signature: Kaleidoscope app name, which was a different brand from the company name Inporia
branding.community_and_virality: Covered by Mashable, Gizmodo, TNW and TechCrunch in 2012. No merch.

brand_strength.rationale: The company name was obscure and the Kaleidoscope name was shared by many unrelated products, but the app earned press.

outcome_analysis: Inporia raised a 1.25 million dollar convertible note seed in May 2011 from NEA, SV Angel, 500 Startups and others, and launched the Kaleidoscope fashion app. The company is recorded as closed but no source states when or why, so the cause is not public and no failure factor is assigned. The category was crowded with Pinterest, Fancy and Snapette.
notes: The YC page states a 1.25 million dollar seed with the same investors. Aggregators disagree (one lists 1 million dollars). YC page says Kaleidoscope launched on Android in February 2011 and iPhone in April 2011, but Mashable and TechCrunch coverage dates the launches to 2012, so launch dates conflict. Sarah Kunst and Simon Ratner are named as team members on the YC page, not as founders. Competitor sources: Decide is dated to the funding article (May 2011, after the W11 batch); Snapette is August 2011, five months after the batch; the Mashable list of rivals is dated April 2012 and was not used. Website is dead.
